News Release
Spain's renewable sector has lost €140 Million to grid constraints as curtailment remains elevated since April 2025 blackout

16 November 2026
6 minute read

Email
Share by email

Renewable curtailment in Spain has remained elevated since the April 2025 grid blackout, costing the sector €140 million in lost revenue and set to worsen further as approximately 10 GW of utility-scale solar connects across the remainder of 2026 and through 2028 into an already congested network, according to new Wood Mackenzie analysis. The incoming capacity is part of a 16 GW wave across the full 2026 to 2028 period, of which a significant portion connected in the first eight months of 2026 alone.
The finding comes from "Spain's Technical Curtailment Crunch: How the Next Wave of Solar Growth Will Impact Trends," a report drawing on nodal-level network modelling across Spain's full transmission system. Redispatch volumes in the technical constraints market have not returned to pre-blackout levels. Uncompensated constrained-off volumes now stand at 4% of available renewable supply year-to-date, dominated by gas being called on to replace solar and wind generation being switched off to manage grid stability.
That national average conceals a sharper picture at the local level. At certain nodes in Extremadura and Murcia, curtailment already exceeds 25% of renewable output. For asset owners at those locations, a quarter of potential generation revenue is not being earned.
"Redispatch volumes in Spain's constraints market have not normalised since the April 2025 blackout, and the numbers explain why," said Agustin Huerga, Research Analyst, European Power and Renewables at Wood Mackenzie. "Nodes in Extremadura and Murcia are losing more than a quarter of potential output. The next 10 GW of solar connecting into already congested corridors will deepen that before it eases. More than 35 GW of the existing fleet can provide dynamic voltage control at no additional cost. Whether curtailment stabilises in 2027 or continues rising depends almost entirely on how fast that capacity is brought to compliance."
If none of the 35 GW of renewables capable of providing dynamic voltage control at no additional cost are brought to compliance, curtailment is forecast to rise 18% over the next two years. That condition, not grid congestion alone, is what determines whether the downside scenario materialises. In that case, total curtailment reaches 6.5 TWh by 2028, against 1.3 TWh in 2023.
The structural cause is a grid that was not designed for the pace or scale of Spain's solar buildout. Congestion that was once wind supply-driven is now solar supply-driven. Roughly half of technical curtailment in 2026 stems not from physical line capacity limits but from synchronous system issues: inertia, short-circuit current, and frequency and voltage control. These are services that gas and nuclear plants provide as a matter of course. Inverter-based solar and wind assets must be specifically configured to replicate them, and a large portion of Spain's existing fleet is not.
Around 7 GW of solar PV and 26 GW of wind capacity require inverter retrofits to provide dynamic voltage control, having been commissioned before Royal Decree 647/2020 came into force. Up to 50% of the existing fleet cannot provide the service without further investment. More than 35 GW can be enabled to do so at no additional cost, and plants that do receive priority of dispatch. Grid operator REE had habilitated 4.2 GW of renewable plants through its habilitación programme by May 2026. The regulatory framework exists. The question is whether the pace of compliance keeps up with the pace of new capacity connecting to the grid.
If it does not, Spain's renewable curtailment targets face a material delivery risk. Wood Mackenzie's base case projects curtailment stabilises in 2027 and 2028, but only if the provision of dynamic voltage control from new and existing renewables keeps pace with the approximately 10 GW of solar capacity still to connect.
Solar-driven grid stress is concentrating geographically around Madrid, Toledo and Cáceres as 3 GW of new solar PV comes online in those corridors. Developers are already responding, siting new projects in lower-resource zones including León, Valladolid, Huesca and Zaragoza, a sign that the investment geography of Spanish solar is shifting in real time.
Grid reinforcement is the structural solution, but a seven-year average lead time from greenfield to completion rules it out as a near-term fix. Battery storage and rising electricity demand carry more weight in the short term. Wood Mackenzie forecasts 10 GW of battery storage operational by 2030, rising to 20 GW in the high case, against a 2025 baseline of 0.2 GW. Over 40 GW of battery storage is under development, with 25 GW holding grid access approval. Demand growth from data centres adds 2.3 GW to the pipeline, with over 2 GW forecast online by 2030. Renewables are expected to resolve half of the enhanced contingency management problem, with synchronous condensers closing the remainder by 2029. Curtailment is projected to fall 30% per year over the outlook if those conditions hold.
Key details:

Spain's renewable sector has lost €140 million in revenue to grid curtailment year-to-date, with constraints remaining elevated since the April 2025 blackout, according to Wood Mackenzie analysis based on REE data (October 2026)
Curtailment exceeds 25% of renewable output at certain nodes in Extremadura and Murcia, against a national average of 4% of available supply year-to-date
If none of the 35 GW of renewables able to provide dynamic voltage control at no additional cost are brought to compliance, curtailment rises 18% over two years and reaches 6.5 TWh by 2028, up from 1.3 TWh in 2023
Up to 50% of Spain's renewable fleet cannot provide dynamic voltage control without inverter investment, yet more than 35 GW can be enabled to do so at no additional cost; whether that capacity is brought to compliance is the single variable determining whether curtailment rises 18% or stabilises through 2028
Wood Mackenzie forecasts 10 GW of battery storage operational in Spain by 2030, rising to 20 GW in the high case, with curtailment projected to fall 30% per year once synchronous condensers are fully operational by 2029

Background
Wood Mackenzie's analysis is conducted at nodal resolution across Spain's full transmission system, capturing localised congestion that national averages do not reflect. The base case does not incorporate planned network development. Any grid reinforcement that materialises represents upside to the base case projections. The 16 GW total capacity figure referenced in this release covers the full 2026 to 2028 period; approximately 10 GW remains to connect from October 2026 through 2028.
